content.summary_of_the_paper: Motion facilitates far-depth estimation while the narrow baselines of stereo help better in near-depth estimation. The authors propose to fuse them using uncertainty for the case of an event stream input. Two new datasets are proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+: Depth from events can mitigate the inherent weakness of frame-based approaches in the presence of motion blur (or even HDR). 

-: There is no justification for any design choice in the architecture which seems unreasonably complex for depth estimation compared to state of the art in event-based stereo.

-: There is no explanation why Laplace density was used for the depth uncertainty instead of Gaussian (I guess because depth uncertainty is not symmetric).

-: The authors claim that it is the first approach that fuses motion and stereo but it is not clear what it means because all event stereo approaches use motion implicitly because the events have been captured at different instances in time.

-: There are two datasets in the literature MVSEC (Zhu et al.) and DSEC (Gehrig et al.). with stereo-event data captured from a moving platform used by hundreds of approaches in the event-based community.

-: Instead, the authors used a synthetic dataset produced by Unity3D without explaining how they produced the events when event simulation is an active research problem.

-: The Kitti data are simulated and should not be called real.

-: A real dataset is mentioned (vidar) but there is no explanation how the ground truth was measured (table 3)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is unreadable. Citations are merged without spaces with the methods and 
the language  needs significant improvement (lack of articles, wrong singular-plural use, sentences starting with "And" or "So", no spaces,  being the main problem).  

Appendices A and B are unreadable due to language issues.


The authors miss to cite and compare with event-based stereo methods like 
*Zhu et al. ECCV 2018, Realtime Time Synchronized Event-based Stereo,
*Rogister et al. 2012 Asynchronous event-based binocular stereo matching,
*Rebecq et al. 2018 Event-based multi-view stereo—3D reconstruction with an event camera in real-time
*Steffen et al. 2019 “Neuromorphic stereo vision: A survey of bioinspired sensors and algorithms
* Zhou et al. 2018 Semi-dense 3D reconstruction with a stereo event camera,
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is not mature for publication. The presentation is confusing due to language but also lack of technical clarity. The main reason for rejection, however, is the use of synthetic datasets while there are standard real datasets with depth ground-truth: MVSEC (Zhu et al.), DSEC (Gehrig et al.), or EVIMO2 (Burner et al.).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a novel method for depth estimation from a stereo pair of spike cameras. The main argument of the paper is that stereo depth networks which use correlational volumes have limitations at long range, while monocular depth methods which directly regress depth do not. As a result, the authors propose to learn the uncertainty for both methods, and fuse the two estimates using the predicted uncertainty at test time. A novel dataset generated in simulation is provided for the evaluation, with stereo spiking cameras, rgb images and ground truth depths. Evaluations are performed against several RGB based stereo and monocular methods on the proposed dataset, where the proposed method outperforms due to the high speed scenes in the dataset causing motion blur in the RGB images. Ablations are also provided demonstrating the performance of the proposed fusion over each individual network.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, I find the two main stories in this paper to be interesting: learning dense depth estimation from spike cameras, and fusing direct regression depth estimation methods with correlational volume depth estimation methods. The authors provide good motivation, and clearly outline the proposed method. A simulated dataset is also provided, and ablations are also performed which show that the proposed method clearly improves over the baseline of each individual network.

However, I find that the stories are a little disjoint, as the uncertainty weighted depth estimation scheme seems to have nothing to do with spike cameras, and could easily have been applied to regular rgb cameras. The network architecture seems fairly standard, and aside from the novel dataset, the application of this method towards spike cameras just seems to make it harder to evaluate in the context of prior works. 

The claims made in this paper seem to be a bit too wide-reaching, with direct comparisons between 'stereo' and 'monocular' methods. However, from what I can tell, there is no information missing from passing in stereo images into a network instead of single monocular images (e.g. the monocular method proposed in this paper could have had stereo images as input with no loss in performance). The authors are likely referring to the difference between correlational volume methods and direct regression methods, but I worry that the claims made (e.g. that stereo methods suffer at long range while monocular methods do not) may mislead readers. It would be clearer if the authors clarify what they mean by 'stereo' and 'monocular', or do away with these terms in favor of the correct ones altogether.

The only experiments with comparisons against the state of the art are on the proposed dataset, which contains only images from a fast (91km/h) moving car. While this is beneficial to demonstrate the benefits of the spike camera over rgb ones, it does not provide the reader with information about the baseline performance of the method on a normal (non-motion blurred) scene. The authors provide experiments on a spiking version of the KITTI dataset, but oddly do not provide numbers to compare against for rgb values.

The authors do not discuss the calibration of the uncertainty in the proposed method. While the networks seem to have learned uncertainties that are beneficial for the final depth estimation task, is it possible that the two networks learn uncertainty values with entirely different ranges? E.g. could the monocular network have uncertainties in [0.1, 0.5], while the stereo network has uncertainties in [0.6, 0.8]? In this case, the monocular network could always seem more confident.

While the proposed method seems to improve overall performance, it seems unnecessarily expensive to have to compute the uncertainty values explicitly and compare them at test time. Is it possible to combine the two depth predictions inside the model, so that they can be optimized by the network directly via the loss? 

Many minor editing errors, spaces missing before most citations, Capitalize 'we' at the start of paragraph 2 in Section 3.2.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall paper is well written, and the overall method is clear. The originality in terms of applying this depth estimation network to spike cameras is good, and the experiments do show that a clear improvement is achieved. However, I'm not sure that there is enough evidence that this method works a) better than prior works on the majority of (non-motion blurred) scenes, or whether it performs significantly worse, b) is a benefit limited only to spike cameras or c) generalizes across training iterations, given the potential calibration issues in the uncertainty.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I see promise in this work, but have several concerns about the claims made, evaluation, and other question about the method. I also think that the overall story is a little disjoint, and could use some more connections between the spike camera motivation and the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose an uncertainty guided depth fusion framework for spike data, consisting of four modules, including neuromorphic encoding module, spike encoder, spike decoder, and uncertainty guided fusion. The authors argue that by fusing the data provided by stereo and monocular depth estimation algorithms they can achieve more accurate results on spiking camera data. They introduce the CitySouke20K dataset and the Spike-Kitti dataset and present some results on these datasets. The authors argue that this is the first paper for fusing stereo and monocular data for depth estimation with spiking cameras.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

S1: a novel dataset for spiking stereo data is introduced, which should be appreciated by the community

S2: the code will be released which should make the results reproducible


Weaknesses:

W1: A practical problem with fusion of the data from multiple cameras is the issue of synchronization between cameras. Would this cause any problems with this algorithm?

W2: Fig 1 , the text is too small and not legible.

W3: should include a list of dvs stereo algorithms as dvs and spiking cameras are highly related

W4: the authors should include a disucssion on power requirements. This is the main reason why we are interested in neuromorphic algorithms, due to their potential for low power requirements.

W5: section 32., "we use a shared...". Capitalize "we"

W6: bold text looks odd

W7: page 6 algorithm: this is rather simplistic. Is an equal weight for both losses fine?

W8: section 4: how appropriate is the use of simulated data? Would real data acquired from an actual live stereo system be better?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has a number of clarity issues which i list above. Overall however I do not feel there is sufficient novelty in the paper for the level of ICLR.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main advantage of the paper is the introduction of novel datasets. However the algorithm feels a bit simplistic. I would have preferred to see a more thorough comparison while running the algorithm on actual live stereo rigs.

content.title: Uncertainty Guided Depth Fusion for Spike Camera
content.TL;DR: We propose a novel uncertainty-guided fusion framework for spike depth estimation.
content.abstract: Neuromorphic spike camera captures visual streams with high frame rate in a bio-inspired way, bringing vast potential in various real-world applications such as autonomous driving.Compared with traditional cameras, spike camera data has an inherent advantage to overcome motion blur, leading to more accurate depth estimation in high-velocity circumstances. However, depth estimation with spike camera remains very challenging when using traditional monocular or stereo depth estimation algorithms, which are based on the photometric consistency. In this paper, we propose a novel and effective approach for spike depth estimation, which fuses the monocular and stereo depth estimation for spike camera based on the uncertainty of the prediction.Our approach is motivated by the fact that stereo spike depth estimation achieves better results in closer range while monocular spike depth estimation obtains better results in farther range. Therefore, we introduce an Uncertainty-Guided Depth Fusion (UGDF) framework with a joint training strategy and estimate the distributed uncertainty to fuse the monocular and stereo results. In order to demonstrate the advantage of spike depth estimation over traditional camera-based depth estimation, we contribute a spike-depth dataset named CitySpike20K, which contains 20K paired samples, for spike depth estimation. We also introduce the Spike-Kitti dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method under real-world scenarios.Extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate our method on CitySpike20K and Spike-Kitti. UGDF achieves state-of-the-art results on both CitySpike20K and Spike-Kitti, surpassing all the monocular or stereo spike depth estimation baselines. To the best of our knowledge, our framework is the first end-to-end dual-task fusion framework for spike camera depth estimation. Code and dataset will be released.
